deck.name: Organic Chemistry I
deck.description: A first-semester review of organic structure, stereochemistry, mechanisms, alkene chemistry, spectroscopy, and laboratory methods.

questions.prompt: How many sigma and pi bonds are in a C=C double bond?
choices: One sigma plus one pi bond
Two pi bonds with no sigma
questions.explanation: A double bond contains one sigma bond and one pi bond.

questions.prompt: A tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups is a:
questions.explanation: Four different substituents make that tetrahedral center stereogenic.

questions.prompt: Which pair are nonsuperimposable mirror images?
questions.explanation: Enantiomers are stereoisomers related as nonsuperimposable mirror images.

questions.prompt: A molecule has stereocenters but is achiral because it has internal symmetry. It is:
questions.explanation: Internal symmetry can make a molecule with stereocenters superimposable on its mirror image.

questions.prompt: What is the lowest-energy staggered conformation of butane around its central bond?
questions.explanation: The anti conformation puts the methyl groups 180° apart, reducing steric repulsion.

questions.prompt: A bulky tert-butyl group on cyclohexane strongly prefers which chair position?
questions.explanation: The equatorial position reduces unfavorable 1,3-diaxial interactions.

questions.prompt: Which substrate is fastest in SN2 with the same nucleophile and leaving group?
questions.explanation: SN2 requires backside approach; the least hindered methyl substrate reacts fastest.

questions.prompt: An SN2 reaction at a stereogenic carbon typically gives:
questions.explanation: Backside attack produces inversion of configuration at the reacting center.

questions.prompt: Which solvent often favors SN2 by leaving anionic nucleophiles relatively reactive?
questions.explanation: Polar aprotic solvents solvate cations without strongly hydrogen-bonding to anionic nucleophiles.

questions.prompt: Which substrate is most favorable for SN1 in a polar protic solvent?
questions.explanation: Ionization gives a relatively stable tertiary carbocation.

questions.prompt: In the simple SN1 model, the rate depends on:
questions.explanation: The rate-determining ionization step involves the substrate alone.

questions.prompt: Which substrate is least suitable for SN2?
questions.explanation: Steric crowding at a tertiary carbon blocks backside approach.

questions.prompt: E2 elimination requires the leaving group and beta hydrogen to be aligned:
questions.explanation: Antiperiplanar bonds align for effective formation of the new pi bond.

questions.prompt: The Zaitsev product is generally the:
questions.explanation: With many small bases, elimination favors the more substituted alkene, subject to substrate and condition effects.

questions.prompt: A bulky base often increases formation of the:
questions.explanation: Steric hindrance can favor removal of a more accessible beta hydrogen.

questions.prompt: Which conditions commonly favor elimination over substitution?
questions.explanation: Strong bulky base and heat often favor elimination; substrate and solvent still matter.

questions.prompt: HBr adds to propene without peroxides mainly to form:
questions.explanation: Ionic Markovnikov addition proceeds through the more stable secondary carbocation.

questions.prompt: Hydroboration-oxidation of a terminal alkene places OH mainly on the:
questions.explanation: The net hydration is anti-Markovnikov and typically avoids a free carbocation.

questions.prompt: Oxymercuration-demercuration gives Markovnikov hydration while avoiding typical:
questions.explanation: A bridged mercurinium intermediate avoids a free carbocation that could rearrange.

questions.prompt: Addition of Br2 to an alkene through a bromonium ion gives mainly:
questions.explanation: Bromide attacks opposite the bridged bromonium ion, giving anti addition.

questions.prompt: Catalytic hydrogenation adds H atoms to an alkene mainly by:
questions.explanation: Both hydrogens are delivered from the catalyst surface to the same face in the standard model.

questions.prompt: Oxidative cleavage of an alkene primarily:
choices: Changes C=C into a single bond
Adds two atoms across the double bond
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis and related methods split the double-bond carbon-carbon bond; workup affects products.

questions.prompt: Which reagent commonly reduces an alkene to an alkane?
questions.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation adds H2 across the double bond.

questions.prompt: A terminal alkyne is more acidic than an alkane because its conjugate base has carbon that is:
questions.explanation: Greater s-character helps stabilize negative charge on the sp-hybridized carbon.

questions.prompt: An acetylide anion most reliably forms a C-C bond by SN2 with a:
questions.explanation: Methyl and primary electrophiles favor substitution over elimination by the strong acetylide base.

questions.prompt: In a radical chain mechanism, the step that first creates radicals is:
questions.explanation: Initiation generates radicals, often through homolytic bond cleavage.

questions.prompt: Which simple alkyl radical is usually most stable?
questions.explanation: Alkyl substitution stabilizes carbon radicals through hyperconjugation and inductive effects.

questions.prompt: A strong IR absorption near 1700 cm-1 often indicates a:
questions.explanation: Carbonyl stretches commonly occur around 1650-1800 cm-1 depending on structure.

questions.prompt: A broad IR feature around 3200-3600 cm-1 often suggests:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded alcohol O-H absorption is often broad in this region.

questions.prompt: In proton NMR, integration is most directly related to:
questions.explanation: Integration estimates relative numbers of protons contributing to each signal.

questions.prompt: By the simple n+1 rule, a proton next to three equivalent hydrogens often gives a:
questions.explanation: Three equivalent neighboring protons split a signal into 3 + 1 = 4 lines.

questions.prompt: In mass spectrometry, m/z means:
questions.explanation: Mass spectrometers separate ions according to mass divided by charge.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives degree of unsaturation for a neutral formula with C,H,N and halogens X?
questions.explanation: Oxygen and sulfur are omitted; each ring or pi bond contributes one degree.

questions.prompt: A C4H10 formula has how many degrees of unsaturation?
questions.explanation: (2×4 + 2 − 10)/2 = 0, consistent with a saturated acyclic formula.

questions.prompt: Which method separates compounds by their interaction with stationary and mobile phases?
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates substances through differential partitioning or adsorption.

questions.prompt: On polar silica TLC with a fixed solvent, which compound often travels farther?
questions.explanation: Less polar analytes often interact less strongly with silica and travel farther.

questions.prompt: Why add a boiling chip before heating a liquid?
choices: Provide nucleation sites and reduce bumping
questions.explanation: Boiling chips promote steady bubble formation and must be added before heating.

questions.prompt: Why can repeated small solvent portions extract more solute than one equal total portion?
questions.explanation: Partition equilibrium makes several fresh extractions more efficient than one large extraction of equal total volume.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of recrystallization?
choices: Separate gases by their molecular masses
Measure reaction rate as products form
Purify a solid using hot-cold solubility differences
Convert an alcohol into a new alkene
questions.explanation: The desired solid dissolves hot and crystallizes as the solution cools.

questions.prompt: Which pair of factors influences SN1 versus SN2 pathway choice?
choices: Oxygen atoms present in the air
questions.explanation: Steric hindrance, carbocation stability, nucleophile, and solvent all matter.

questions.prompt: A nucleophile is best described as an:
questions.explanation: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a bond.

questions.prompt: In a curved-arrow mechanism, the arrow tail begins at:
choices: A positive charge with no electrons
questions.explanation: Curved arrows track electron-pair movement from an electron source.

questions.prompt: Which feature stabilizes a carbocation?
questions.explanation: Resonance spreads the positive charge over more than one atom.

questions.prompt: Why can rearrangement occur in some SN1 reactions?
choices: A carbocation can shift to a more stable position
questions.explanation: Hydride or alkyl shifts can relocate the charge to a more stable carbocation.

questions.prompt: E/Z isomerism is possible when each alkene carbon has:
questions.explanation: Distinct substituents and restricted double-bond rotation allow E/Z forms.

questions.prompt: What prevents free rotation around a carbon-carbon double bond?
questions.explanation: Rotation would disrupt side-on overlap that forms the pi bond.

questions.prompt: If high-priority groups lie on opposite sides of C=C, the configuration is:
questions.explanation: E denotes opposite sides; Z denotes the same side.

questions.prompt: A racemic mixture contains:
questions.explanation: Equal enantiomer rotations cancel in bulk under the same conditions.

questions.prompt: Which alkene reaction produces a vicinal dihalide?
questions.explanation: Each of the two formerly alkene carbons receives a halogen atom.

questions.prompt: A strong IR peak at 1715 cm-1 with no broad O-H band most supports a:
questions.explanation: A saturated ketone commonly has a strong carbonyl stretch near this value.

questions.prompt: An aldehyde proton often appears in proton NMR near:
questions.explanation: Aldehyde protons are strongly deshielded and commonly appear around 9-10 ppm.

questions.prompt: On a reaction coordinate diagram, a transition state is at a:
questions.explanation: A transition state is a maximum; an intermediate is a local minimum between steps.

questions.prompt: An exothermic reaction has products with:
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat and have negative enthalpy change.

questions.prompt: Which alkene hydration method is most prone to carbocation rearrangement?
questions.explanation: Acid-catalyzed hydration passes through a carbocation intermediate.

questions.prompt: Mild oxidation of a primary alcohol can stop at an:
questions.explanation: With a suitable mild oxidant, a primary alcohol can be oxidized to an aldehyde.

questions.prompt: An electrophile is an electron-pair:
questions.explanation: Electrophiles are electron-poor sites that accept an electron pair from a nucleophile.

questions.prompt: A pi bond forms by side-by-side overlap of p orbitals.
questions.explanation: Side-on overlap places electron density above and below the bond axis.

questions.prompt: Every molecule with a stereocenter must be chiral.
questions.explanation: Internal symmetry can make a molecule with stereocenters achiral.

questions.prompt: A cyclohexane chair flip switches axial and equatorial positions but retains up/down orientation.
questions.explanation: Each substituent changes axial/equatorial status while keeping its up/down direction.

questions.prompt: SN2 proceeds through a long-lived planar carbocation.
questions.explanation: SN2 is concerted and does not form a discrete carbocation.

questions.prompt: Increasing steric hindrance at the reacting carbon generally slows SN2.
questions.explanation: Crowding blocks the nucleophile’s backside approach.

questions.prompt: A tertiary alkyl halide usually undergoes SN2 faster than a methyl halide.
questions.explanation: Methyl substrates are least hindered; tertiary centers strongly block SN2.

questions.prompt: In the simple SN1 model, the rate depends on nucleophile concentration.
questions.explanation: The rate-determining ionization depends on substrate concentration.

questions.prompt: SN1 substitution at a stereogenic center may give a mixture of configurations.
questions.explanation: A planar carbocation can be attacked from either face, often with partial racemization.

questions.prompt: E2 involves removal of a beta hydrogen as the leaving group departs in one concerted step.
questions.explanation: The bond changes occur together as the new pi bond forms.

questions.prompt: E2 elimination requires a beta hydrogen.
questions.explanation: The base removes a beta hydrogen while the leaving group departs from the adjacent carbon.

questions.prompt: Zaitsev product means the less substituted alkene.
questions.explanation: The Zaitsev product is generally the more substituted alkene.

questions.prompt: HBr addition to an alkene is always anti-Markovnikov without peroxides.
questions.explanation: Ordinary ionic addition is Markovnikov; radical anti-Markovnikov addition uses peroxide conditions.

questions.prompt: Hydroboration-oxidation gives net anti-Markovnikov hydration.
questions.explanation: OH ends up on the less substituted carbon.

questions.prompt: A bromonium ion intermediate helps explain anti addition of Br2 to an alkene.
questions.explanation: The bridged ion is attacked from the opposite face.

questions.prompt: Catalytic hydrogenation turns an alkene C=C into a C-C single bond.
questions.explanation: H atoms add across the pi bond.

questions.prompt: Carbonyl groups typically absorb only below 1000 cm-1 in an IR spectrum.
questions.explanation: Carbonyl stretches usually occur around 1650-1800 cm-1.

questions.prompt: In proton NMR, integration estimates relative numbers of contributing hydrogens.
questions.explanation: Integrals are normalized to relative proton counts.

questions.prompt: Two equivalent neighboring protons often split a signal into a triplet in a simple first-order spectrum.
questions.explanation: The simple n+1 rule gives 2+1 lines.

questions.prompt: Mass spectrometry separates ions according to mass-to-charge ratio.
questions.explanation: Detected ions are distinguished by their m/z values.

questions.prompt: One ring or one pi bond contributes one degree of unsaturation.
questions.explanation: A triple bond contributes two degrees.

questions.prompt: Silica gel is a common polar stationary phase in TLC.
questions.explanation: Silica’s polarity affects how strongly different analytes are retained.

questions.prompt: A catalyst changes a reaction’s equilibrium position.
questions.explanation: A catalyst changes rates but not the equilibrium constant or position.

questions.prompt: What is a sigma bond?
questions.answer: A covalent bond with electron density concentrated along the internuclear axis.
questions.explanation: A single bond is one sigma bond.

questions.prompt: What is a pi bond?
questions.answer: A bond from side-by-side p-orbital overlap, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis.
questions.explanation: Pi bonds accompany sigma bonds in double and triple bonds.

questions.prompt: What does a curved arrow mean in an organic mechanism?
questions.answer: Movement of an electron pair from a source such as a lone pair or bond to a new location.
questions.explanation: The tail begins at the electron source.

questions.prompt: What is a nucleophile?
questions.answer: An electron-pair donor that forms a bond to an electrophilic site.
questions.explanation: Nucleophiles may be neutral or negatively charged.

questions.prompt: What is an electrophile?
questions.answer: An electron-pair acceptor that reacts with a nucleophile.
questions.explanation: Carbocations and polarized carbonyl carbons are examples.

questions.prompt: What is a carbocation?
questions.answer: An organic species with a positively charged carbon center.
questions.explanation: Resonance or alkyl substitution can stabilize a carbocation.

questions.prompt: What defines SN2?
questions.answer: A concerted substitution where nucleophile attack and leaving-group departure occur in one step, usually with inversion.
questions.explanation: The simple rate law depends on both substrate and nucleophile.

questions.prompt: What defines SN1?
questions.answer: Substitution through ionization to a carbocation, followed by nucleophile capture.
questions.explanation: The simple rate-determining step depends on substrate concentration.

questions.prompt: What defines E2?
questions.answer: A concerted elimination where a base removes a beta hydrogen as the leaving group departs and a pi bond forms.
questions.explanation: Antiperiplanar geometry is often important.

questions.prompt: What does Markovnikov orientation predict for HX addition to an unsymmetrical alkene?
questions.answer: H generally adds to the carbon already bearing more H atoms; X adds to the more substituted carbon.
questions.explanation: The pattern often follows formation of the more stable carbocation.

questions.prompt: What is anti-Markovnikov hydration by hydroboration-oxidation?
questions.answer: Alkene hydration that places OH on the less substituted carbon, with net syn addition of H and OH.
questions.explanation: The reaction avoids a free carbocation intermediate.

questions.prompt: What does anti addition mean?
questions.answer: Two groups add to opposite faces of a double bond.
questions.explanation: Bromination through a bromonium ion is a common example.

questions.prompt: What is the anti conformation of butane?
questions.answer: A staggered arrangement with methyl groups 180 degrees apart.
questions.explanation: It is the lowest-energy staggered conformation.

questions.prompt: What is a meso compound?
questions.answer: An achiral molecule with stereocenters whose internal symmetry makes it superimposable on its mirror image.
questions.explanation: A meso compound is one compound, not a racemic mixture.

questions.prompt: What do E and Z describe?
questions.answer: The relative positions of high-priority substituents on a double bond: opposite for E and same side for Z.
questions.explanation: CIP priority rules identify the high-priority substituent on each carbon.

questions.prompt: What is a racemic mixture?
questions.answer: An equal mixture of two enantiomers.
questions.explanation: Their optical rotations cancel in bulk.

questions.prompt: What does proton NMR integration show?
questions.answer: Relative numbers of hydrogens contributing to each signal.
questions.explanation: Integration complements chemical-shift and splitting data.

questions.prompt: What is the simple n+1 splitting rule?
questions.answer: A proton set with n equivalent neighboring hydrogens often appears as n+1 lines in a simple first-order spectrum.
questions.explanation: The rule has limits for coupled nonequivalent protons.

questions.prompt: What is the degree of unsaturation?
questions.answer: A count of rings and pi bonds implied by a molecular formula relative to a saturated acyclic formula.
questions.explanation: A ring or double bond contributes one; a triple bond contributes two.

questions.prompt: What is recrystallization used for?
questions.answer: Purifying a solid by using its temperature-dependent solubility in a suitable solvent.
questions.explanation: The compound dissolves hot and crystallizes as the solution cools.

questions.prompt: In IUPAC naming, the parent chain is generally chosen as the longest chain that:
choices: Includes the highest-priority group and most unsaturation
Has the greatest number of branches only
Begins at the left side of the drawing
Contains only primary carbons in sequence
questions.explanation: Parent-chain selection follows priority rules, including the principal functional group and unsaturation.

questions.prompt: What is the functional group in an ether?
choices: An oxygen bonded to two carbon groups
questions.explanation: Ethers have the general structure R-O-R prime.

questions.prompt: Which group distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?
choices: A carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbons
A terminal carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen
questions.explanation: An aldehyde has at least one hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon; a ketone has two carbon substituents.

questions.prompt: In an E1 reaction, the slow step usually forms a:
choices: Pi bond by one concerted step
Carbocation by loss of the leaving group
questions.explanation: The rate-determining ionization generates a carbocation before deprotonation forms the alkene.

questions.prompt: Which compound is more acidic, using typical pKa values?
choices: A carboxylic acid with pKa near 5
questions.explanation: Lower pKa corresponds to a stronger acid; carboxylate resonance stabilizes the conjugate base.

questions.prompt: Which method is used to assign R or S configuration at a tetrahedral stereocenter?
questions.explanation: CIP priorities are ranked by atomic number, then the lowest-priority group is oriented away.

questions.prompt: A Newman projection looks along which bond?
questions.explanation: The front and rear atoms show the conformation around a selected single bond.

questions.prompt: Which IR feature is typical of a nitrile C≡N stretch?
choices: A broad band near 3300 cm-1 only
questions.explanation: Nitrile triple-bond stretching commonly appears around 2200-2300 cm-1.

questions.prompt: An E1 reaction proceeds through a carbocation intermediate.
questions.explanation: The leaving group departs before the base removes a beta proton.

questions.prompt: A lower pKa indicates a stronger acid.
questions.explanation: Acid strength increases as pKa decreases.

questions.prompt: A ketone carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes a ketone from an aldehyde, which has at least one hydrogen at the carbonyl carbon.

questions.prompt: How is an ether functional group written?
questions.answer: R-O-R prime: an oxygen bonded to two carbon groups.
questions.explanation: The oxygen is not part of a carbonyl in a simple ether.

questions.prompt: How does an aldehyde differ from a ketone?
questions.answer: An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen; a ketone has two carbon substituents.
questions.explanation: Both contain a carbonyl group.

questions.prompt: What is an E1 reaction?
questions.answer: A two-step elimination in which the leaving group first forms a carbocation, then a base removes a beta hydrogen to make an alkene.
questions.explanation: Its rate in the simple model depends on substrate concentration.

questions.prompt: What does a Newman projection show?
questions.answer: The three-dimensional arrangement of groups when looking along a selected single bond.
questions.explanation: It is used to compare eclipsed and staggered conformations.

questions.prompt: What do R and S label?
questions.answer: The absolute configuration at a stereogenic center using Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priorities.
questions.explanation: R and S labels are assigned from the ranked substituent order with the lowest priority directed away.
